Turn to the Lord before it is too late (verses 1–6)

God's almighty power and sovereign rule should move sinners to repent and return to him.

How desirable it is to have the Lord of hosts as our Friend, and how dreadful to have him as our enemy!

Consider what happened to earlier generations and the warnings God sent them through his prophets.

The only way to escape approaching ruin is to abandon our evil ways.

Where are our fathers, and where are the prophets who preached to them?

They once walked through the same streets, lived in the same houses, worked in the same shops and worshiped in the same places as we do.

Now they have all passed away.

But dying did not end their existence.

They have entered the unchanging world of eternity, toward which we are rapidly traveling.

Those who lived and died in sin are under judgment; those who lived and died in Christ are in heaven.

If we live and die as they did, we will soon join them in one condition or the other.

The disregard of earlier generations for their own souls gives us no reason to ruin ours.

Their prophets also died.

Jesus Christ alone is the Prophet who lives forever; the ministries of all other prophets have an appointed end.

What a serious thing it is that dying ministers speak to dying hearers about souls that never die!

Both stand on eternity's threshold.

The preachers died, and those who heard them died.

But God's word did not die.

Not one part of it fell to the ground, because God is righteous and faithful.

The vision of the horsemen and the angels (verses 7–17)

Zechariah saw a dark grove of myrtle trees, sheltered by hills.

It pictured the low and distressed condition of the Jewish church.

Among those trees was a warrior on a red horse.

Henry understands this figure as Christ present among his suffering people, ready to come to their help.

Behind him stood angels, ready to carry out his purposes—some through judgment, others through mercy, and others through events containing both.

To understand the mysteries of God's kingdom, we should turn not to angels but to Christ himself.

Angels also have things to learn.

The Savior gladly teaches those who humbly wish to understand the things of God.

The nations around Judah were at peace, while the returned Jews still experienced insecurity.

This contrast prompted the intercession in the vision.

But mercy must be sought through Christ, whose prayer for his church prevails.

The Lord answered the Angel of the Covenant with good and comforting promises.

All the gospel's gracious promises come to us from Jesus Christ, who receives them from his Father in response to the intercession of his blood.

Ministers are to declare those promises throughout the world.

It is not unusual for God's enemies to enjoy worldly rest while his people undergo discipline, temptation, fear, oppression and persecution.

The prophecy offered hope for the revival of the Jews after their captivity.

Henry also regards those events as shadows of the future restoration of the church after the oppression of “New Testament Babylon” has ended.

That later application is Henry's interpretive expectation, not a newly established historical fulfillment.

The four horns and the workmen (verses 18–21)

The church's enemies aimed to erase Israel's name.

The four horns symbolized power, strength and violent hostility.

At first the prophet saw them as so formidable that the safety of every faithful person and the success of every good work seemed doubtful.

Then the Lord showed him four workmen empowered to break the horns.

Our physical eyes see the dangers that surround God's church.

Whichever way we look, we see the power of those who oppose it.

But only the eyes of faith see that the church is safe under God's protection.

When the Lord has work to accomplish, he will raise up people to do it.

He will also provide others to defend the workers and protect the work.

How much reason we have to praise the holy and eternal Spirit, who cares for the present and eternal welfare of believers and, through God's word, teaches the church the wonders of salvation!
classic_reading:
[Zech.1.1-Zech.1.6]
Zechariah
This prophecy is suitable to all, as the scope is to reprove for sin, and threaten God's judgments against the impenitent, and to encourage those that feared God, with assurances of the mercy God had in store for his church, and especially of the coming of the Messiah, and the setting up his kingdom in the world.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
An exhortation to repentance. | (1-6) |
A vision of the ministry of angels. | (7-17) |
The security of the Jews and the destruction of their enemies. | (18-21) |
Verses 1-6
God's almighty power and sovereign dominion, should engage and encourage sinners to repent and turn to Him. It is very desirable to have the Lord of hosts for our friend, and very dreadful to have him for our enemy. Review what is past, and observe the message God sent by his servants, the prophets, to your fathers. Turn ye now from your evil ways, and from your evil doings. Be persuaded to leave your sins, as the only way to prevent approaching ruin. What is become of our fathers, and of the prophets that preached to them? They are all dead and gone. Here they were, in the towns and countries where we live, passing and repassing in the same streets, dwelling in the same houses, trading in the same shops and exchanges, worshipping God in the same places. But where are they? When they died, there was not an end of them; they are in eternity, in the world of spirits, the unchangeable world to which we hasten apace. Where are they? Those of them who lived and died in sin, are in torment. Those who lived and died in Christ, are in heaven; and if we live and die as they did, we shall be with them shortly and eternally. If they minded not their own souls, is that a reason why their posterity should ruin theirs also? The prophets are gone. Christ is a Prophet that lives for ever, but all other prophets have a period put to their office. Oh that this consideration had its due weight; that dying ministers are dealing with dying people about their never-dying souls, and an awful eternity, upon the brink of which both are standing! In another world, both we and our prophets shall live for ever: to prepare for that world ought to be our great care in this. The preachers died, and the hearers died, but the word of God died not; not one jot or title of it fell to the ground; for he is righteous.
[Zech.1.7-Zech.1.17]
Verses 7-17
The prophet saw a dark, shady grove, hidden by hills. This represented the low, melancholy condition of the Jewish church. A man like a warrior sat on a red horse, in the midst of this shady myrtle-grove. Though the church was in a low condition, Christ was present in the midst, ready to appear for the relief of his people. Behind him were angels ready to be employed by him, some in acts of judgment, others of mercy, others in mixed events. Would we know something of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, we must apply, not to angels, for they are themselves learners, but to Christ himself. He is ready to teach those humbly desirous to learn the things of God. The nations near Judea enjoyed peace at that time, but the state of the Jews was unsettled, which gave rise to the pleading that followed; but mercy must only be hoped for through Christ. His intercession for his church prevails. The Lord answered the Angel, this Angel of the covenant, with promises of mercy and deliverance. All the good words and comfortable words of the gospel we receive from Jesus Christ, as he received them from the Father, in answer to the prayer of his blood; and his ministers are to preach them to all the world. The earth sat still, and was at rest. It is not uncommon for the enemies of God to be at rest in sin, while his people are enduring correction, harassed by temptation, disquieted by fears of wrath, or groaning under oppression and persecution. Here are predictions which had reference to the revival of the Jews after the captivity, but those events were shadows of what shall take place in the church, after the oppression of the New Testament Babylon is ended.
[Zech.1.18-Zech.1.21]
Verses 18-21
The enemies of the church threaten to cut off the name of Israel. They are horns, emblems of power, strength, and violence. The prophet saw them so formidable that he began to despair of the safety of every good man, and the success of every good work; but the Lord showed him four workmen empowered to cut off these horns. With an eye of sense we see the power of the enemies of the church; look which way we will, the world shows us that; but it is only with an eye of faith that we see it safe. The Lord shows us that. When God has work to do, he will raise up some to do it, and others to defend it, and to protect those employed in doing it. What cause there is to look up in love and praise to the holy and eternal Spirit, who has the same care over the present and eternal interests of believers, by the holy word bringing the church to know the wonderful things of salvation!

The Lord surrounds his growing city (verses 1–5)

The man with the measuring line is, in Henry's reading, the Son of David, Jesus Christ.

He is the Master Builder of his church.

God knows the extent of his church and will ensure that every guest invited to the wedding supper has a place.

Jerusalem's enlargement is a gracious promise.

City walls normally protect the inhabitants but also limit the room available to them.

This Jerusalem would be as spacious as a city without walls, yet as secure as a city with the strongest walls.

There is room for multitudes no person can number.

No one who trusts in Christ will be refused.

The Lord never shuts out of heaven a genuine member of his church on earth.

God himself will be a wall of fire around his people.

No enemy can break through, undermine or attack such a wall without facing danger.

Henry sees this vision finding its fuller accomplishment in the gospel church, enlarged by the admission of the Gentiles and protected by the Son of God, especially during the glorious days still to come.

The people are called to leave Babylon (verses 6–9)

If the Lord builds Jerusalem for his people, they should inhabit it for his glory.

The privileges and promises of life among God's people should persuade us to join them whatever the cost.

When Zion is being enlarged to receive all God's Israel, remaining in Babylon is foolish.

We must not remain willingly captive to sin, even when worldly circumstances are comfortable.

Escape for your life; do not look back.

Jesus Christ has announced freedom for captives and has accomplished that deliverance himself.

Everyone should resolve that sin will no longer rule over them.

Those who wish to belong to God's children should separate from this corrupt world (Acts 2:40).

Christ's care for his church displays God's tender love.

Whoever touches the church touches the apple of God's eye—its most sensitive and precious part.

The slightest attack is a serious offense to him.

Christ has been sent as the Protector of his church.

God promises to dwell among his people (verses 10–13)

Henry understands the promise as announcing Christ's coming in human nature.

Many nations would turn away from idols.

God would acknowledge as his own everyone who sincerely joined himself to the Lord.

The passage announces glorious days for Christ's kingdom.

God is about to do something extraordinary and unexpected.

He will take up the cause of a people who seemed long neglected.

Meanwhile we are to submit quietly to his holy will and wait patiently for the outcome.

We may be certain that God will complete all the work he has begun.

In due time he will come to judge, finish saving his people and punish the inhabitants of the world for their sins.
classic_reading:
[Zech.2.1-Zech.2.5]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The prosperity of Jerusalem. | (1-5) |
The Jews called to return to their own land. | (6-9) |
A promise of God's presence. | (10-13) |
Verses 1-5
The Son of David, even the Man Christ Jesus, whom the prophet sees with a measuring line in his hand, is the Master-Builder of his church. God notices the extent of his church, and will take care that whatever number of guests are brought to the wedding-supper, there shall be room. This vision means well to Jerusalem. The walls of a city, as they defend it, so they straiten its inhabitants; but Jerusalem shall be extended as freely as if it had no walls at all, yet shall be as safe as if it had the strongest walls. In the church of God there yet is room for other multitudes, more than man can number. None shall be refused who trust in Christ; and He never shuts out from heaven one true member of the church on earth. God will be a Wall of fire round them, which can neither be broken through nor undermined, nor can it be assailed without danger to those who attack. This vision was to have its full accomplishment in the gospel church, which is extended by admitting the Gentiles into it; and which has the Son of God for its Prince and Protector; especially in the glorious times yet to come.
[Zech.2.6-Zech.2.9]
Verses 6-9
If God will build Jerusalem for the people and their comfort, they must inhabit it for him and his glory. The promises and privileges with which God's people are blessed, should engage us to join them, whatever it costs us. When Zion is enlarged to make room for all God's Israel, it is the greatest madness for any of them to stay in Babylon. The captivity of a sinful state is by no means to be continued in, though a man may be easy in worldly matters. Escape for thy life, look not behind thee. Christ has proclaimed that deliverance to the captives, which he has himself wrought out, and it concerns every one to resolve that sin shall not have dominion over him. Those who would be found among God's children, must save themselves from this world, see [Acts.2.40] Ac 2:40. What Christ will do for his church, shall be an evident proof of God's care and affection. He that touches you, touches the apple of his eye. This is a strong expression of God's love to his church. He takes what is done against her as done against the tenderest part of the eye, to which the least touch is a great offence. Christ is sent to be the Protector of his church.
[Zech.2.10-Zech.2.13]
Verses 10-13
Here is a prediction of the coming of Christ in human nature. Many nations in that day would renounce idolatry, and God will own those for his people who join him with purpose of heart. Glorious times are foretold as a prophecy of our Lord's coming and kingdom. God is about to do something unexpected, and very surprising, and to plead his people's cause, which had long seemed neglected. Silently submit to his holy will, and patiently wait the event; assured that God will complete all his work. He will ere long come to judgment, to complete the salvation of his people, and to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their sins.

Joshua is cleansed and restored (verses 1–5)

Zechariah saw Joshua the high priest standing before the Lord, accused by Satan.

Both guilt and corruption make it difficult for sinners to approach a holy God.

Because of the sins we have committed, we are liable to his justice.

Because sin still lives and works within us, we are offensive to his holiness.

Even God's people face these dangers.

Their remedy is Jesus Christ, whom God has made both righteousness and sanctification for them.

Joshua stood accused but was justified.

When we seek to worship God or serve him publicly, we should expect Satan's malice and cleverness to oppose us.

But Satan is rebuked by the One who has conquered him.

Those belonging to Christ will find him ready to defend them when the accusation is fiercest.

A converted soul is a burning brand pulled from the fire through a miracle of free grace.

Christ will not leave such a person to Satan.

Joshua appeared polluted, but he was cleansed.

He represented God's people, who remain unclean until they are washed and sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of God.

Israel had now turned away from idolatry, yet much was still wrong.

Enemies within their spiritual lives were even more dangerous than hostile neighboring nations.

Christ detested the filth on Joshua's garments but did not reject Joshua.

He acts this way toward people chosen to serve him as priests.

Pardoning mercy removes the guilt of sin. Renewing grace breaks sin's power.

Christ washes sinners in his own blood and makes them kings and priests to God.

Those he appoints as spiritual priests stand before God clothed in the spotless robe of Christ's righteousness and adorned with the graces of his Spirit.

The righteousness of the saints is both imputed and implanted.

It is pictured by the clean white linen worn by the Lamb's bride (Revelation 19:8).

Joshua was restored to his former honor and responsibilities.

The crown of the priesthood was placed on him again.

When God intends to revive true religion, he moves prophets and people to pray for that renewal.

The Branch of righteousness and forgiveness in one day (verses 6–10)

God equips those he calls to his service, finding them fit or making them so.

He removes believers' sins through sanctifying grace and enables them to walk in newness of life.

Just as promises to David often become promises about the Messiah, promises to Joshua point to Christ, whose priesthood Joshua's foreshadowed.

Whatever trials or duties we face, our dependence must rest upon Christ, the Branch of righteousness.

Christ is God's Servant, carrying out his Father's work, obeying his will and living for his glory.

He is the Branch from whom all our spiritual fruit comes.

His Father's eye rested upon him, especially in his suffering.

Henry observes that Christ was hidden in the grave like a foundation stone buried from sight, but adds an important qualification: the prophecy more directly describes the attention given to this precious Cornerstone.

Believers before the Savior's coming looked toward him through types and promises.

Believers after his coming look to him with faith, hope and love.

Christ appears for his chosen people like the high priest carrying Israel's names on the stones of his breastplate.

God has given the redeemed to Christ to bring them by grace to glory.

Through Christ both sin's guilt and its dominion are removed.

The decisive work was accomplished in one day—the day he suffered and died.

Once sin is taken away, nothing can ultimately destroy those sheltered by the Savior.

They can rest joyfully under his protection.

And when gospel grace works powerfully in hearts, it makes people eager to invite others to share that blessing.
classic_reading:
[Zech.3.1-Zech.3.5]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The restoration of the church. | (1-5) |
A promise concerning the Messiah. | (6-10) |
Verses 1-5
The angel showed Joshua, the high priest, to Zechariah, in a vision. Guilt and corruption are great discouragements when we stand before God. By the guilt of the sins committed by us, we are liable to the justice of God; by the power of sin that dwells in us, we are hateful to the holiness of God. Even God's Israel are in danger on these accounts; but they have relief from Jesus Christ, who is made of God to us both righteousness and sanctification. Joshua, the high priest, is accused as a criminal, but is justified. When we stand before God, to minister to him, or stand up for God, we must expect to meet all the resistance Satan's subtlety and malice can give. Satan is checked by one that has conquered him, and many times silenced him. Those who belong to Christ, will find him ready to appear for them, when Satan appears most strongly against them. A converted soul is a brand plucked out of the fire by a miracle of free grace, therefore shall not be left a prey to Satan. Joshua appears as one polluted, but is purified; he represents the Israel of God, who are all as an unclean thing, till they are washed and sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God. Israel now were free from idolatry, but there were many things amiss in them. There were spiritual enemies warring against them, more dangerous than any neighbouring nations. Christ loathed the filthiness of Joshua's garments, yet did not put him away. Thus God by his grace does with those whom he chooses to be priests to himself. The guilt of sin is taken away by pardoning mercy, and the power of it is broken by renewing grace. Thus Christ washes those from their sins in his own blood, whom he makes kings and priests to our God. Those whom Christ makes spiritual priests, are clothed with the spotless robe of his righteousness, and appear before God in that; and with the graces of his Spirit, which are ornaments to them. The righteousness of saints, both imputed and implanted, is the fine linen, clean and white, with which the bride, the Lamb's wife, is arrayed, [Rev.19.8] Re 19:8. Joshua is restored to former honours and trusts. The crown of the priesthood is put on him. When the Lord designs to restore and revive religion, he stirs up prophets and people to pray for it.
[Zech.3.6-Zech.3.10]
Verses 6-10
All whom God calls to any office he finds fit, or makes so. The Lord will cause the sins of the believer to pass away by his sanctifying grace, and will enable him to walk in newness of life. As the promises made to David often pass into promises of the Messiah, so the promises to Joshua look forward to Christ, of whose priesthood Joshua's was a shadow. Whatever trials we pass through, whatever services we perform, our whole dependence must rest on Christ, the Branch of righteousness. He is God's servant, employed in his work, obedient to his will, devoted to his honour and glory. He is the Branch from which all our fruit must be gathered. The eye of his Father was upon him, especially in his sufferings, and when he was buried in the grave, as the foundation-stones are under ground, out of men's sight. But the prophecy rather denotes the attention paid to this precious Corner-stone. All believers, from the beginning, had looked forward to it in the types and predictions. All believers, after Christ's coming, would look to it with faith, hope, and love. Christ shall appear for all his chosen, as the high priest when before the Lord, with the names of all Israel graven in the precious stones of his breastplate. When God gave a remnant to Christ, to be brought through grace to glory, then he engraved this precious stone. By him sin shall be taken away, both the guilt and the dominion of it; he did it in one day, that day in which he suffered and died. What should terrify when sin is taken away? Then nothing can hurt, and we sit down under Christ's shadow with delight, and are sheltered by it. And gospel grace, coming with power, makes men forward to draw others to it.

The lampstand and the two olive trees (verses 1–7)

The prophet's spirit wanted to listen, but his body was weak.

We should ask God to awaken us whenever he speaks and then rouse ourselves to pay attention.

The church is like a golden lampstand set in this dark world to give light through God's revelation.

Two olive trees stood beside it, supplying a continuous stream of oil.

The Lord brings his gracious purposes for his church to completion without depending upon human skill or labor.

Sometimes he employs human instruments, but he does not need them.

The oil pictured the abundance of grace by which he brings light and holiness to the church's ministers and members.

No human power can produce that grace or stop it from being given.

The temple's construction would therefore reach a happy conclusion.

All the difficulties were pictured as a great mountain.

Through faith, they would be brought down and made level.

Christ is our Zerubbabel.

He has encountered mountains of obstacles, but nothing is too difficult for him.

What began through God's grace can safely be entrusted to that same grace.

He will not abandon the work of his own hands.

Do not despise small beginnings (verses 8–10)

The precise fulfillment of Scripture's prophecies testifies to their divine origin.

God often chooses people who appear weak or unlikely to accomplish great things.

Therefore do not despise the dawning light.

It will grow brighter until the day reaches its fullness.

Those who feared the temple could never be completed would rejoice when they saw Zerubbabel with the plumb line, directing and supervising its completion.

The all-wise and almighty Providence that rules the earth cares particularly for the church.

Everyone carrying responsibility for the work must look to the Lord, remain aware of his Providence, depend upon his guidance and submit to the way he orders events.

Fix your faith upon Christ.

See him carrying out his work according to his glorious plan and each day bringing his spiritual building closer to completion.

The oil supplied through the Lord's anointed (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.11-Zech.4.14" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 11–14</reference>)

Zechariah wanted to understand the two olive trees.

Henry identifies them with Zerubbabel and Joshua, the prince and the priest.

Both had received gifts and grace from the Holy Spirit.

They lived at the same time and served together in God's work.

They foreshadowed Christ's offices of King and Priest.

Those two offices are united in the one person of Jesus Christ, God and man, from whose fullness all grace is received and shared.

The two leaders helped build God's temple.

Christ builds God's church spiritually.

He is not only the Messiah, the Anointed One.

He is also the Good Olive Tree of his church, supplying its needs from his inexhaustible fullness.

The Holy Spirit is the anointing believers receive.

Through the Spirit, all the golden oil of grace flows from Christ to believers and keeps their lamps burning.

Let us seek, through the Savior's intercession and generosity, the supplies of grace that have always been sufficient for his saints in every trial and task.

Let us wait on him through his appointed ordinances, praying to be sanctified completely—in body, soul and spirit.
classic_reading:
[Zech.4.1-Zech.4.7]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
A vision of a candlestick, with two olive trees. | (1-7) |
Further encouragement. | (8-10) |
An explanation respecting the olive trees. | (11-14) |
Verses 1-7
The prophet's spirit was willing to attend, but the flesh was weak. We should beg of God that, whenever he speaks to us, he would awaken us, and we should then stir up ourselves. The church is a golden candlestick, or lamp-bearer, set up for enlightening this dark world, and holding forth the light of Divine revelation. Two olive trees were seen, one on each side the candlestick, from which oil flowed into the bowl without ceasing. God brings to pass his gracious purposes concerning his church, without any art or labour of man; sometimes he makes use of his instruments, yet he needs them not. This represented the abundance of Divine grace, for the enlightening and making holy the ministers and members of the church, and which cannot be procured or prevented by any human power. The vision assures us that the good work of building the temple, should be brought to a happy end. The difficulty is represented as a great mountain. But all difficulties shall vanish, and all the objections be got over. Faith will remove mountains, and make them plains. Christ is our Zerubbabel; mountains of difficulty were in the way of his undertaking, but nothing is too hard for him. What comes from the grace of God, may, in faith, be committed to the grace of God, for he will not forsake the work of his own hands.
[Zech.4.8-Zech.4.10]
Verses 8-10
The exact fulfilment of Scripture prophecies is a convincing proof of their Divine original. Though the instruments be weak and unlikely, yet God often chooses such, to bring about great things by them. Let not the dawning light be despised; it will shine more and more to the perfect day. Those who despaired of finishing the work, shall rejoice when they see Zerubbabel giving directions what to do, and taking care that the work be done. It is a comfort to us that the same all-wise, almighty Providence, which governs the earth, is in particular conversant about the church. All that have the plummet in their hands, must look up to the eyes of the Lord, have constant regard to Divine Providence, act in dependence on its guidance and submission to its disposals. Let us fix our faith on Christ, and view Him carrying on his work according to his own glorious plan, and daily bringing his spiritual building nearer to completion. ( [Zech.4.11-Zech.4.14] Zec 4:11-14)
[Zech.4.11-Zech.4.14]
Verses 11-14
Zechariah desires to know what are the two olive trees. Zerubbabel and Joshua, this prince and this priest, were endued with the gifts and graces of God's Spirit. They lived at the same time, and both were instruments in the work and service of God. Christ's offices of King and Priest were shadowed forth by them. From the union of these two offices in his person, both God and man, the fullness of grace is received and imparted. They built the temple, the church of God. So does Christ spiritually. Christ is not only the Messiah, the Anointed One himself, but he is the Good Olive to his church; and from his fulness we receive. And the Holy Spirit is the unction or anointing which we have received. From Christ the Olive Tree, by the Spirit the Olive Branch, all the golden oil of grace flows to believers, which keeps their lamps burning. Let us seek, through the intercession and bounty of the Saviour, supplies from that fulness which has hitherto sufficed for all his saints, according to their trials and employments. Let us wait on him in his ordinances, desiring to be sanctified wholly in body, soul, and spirit.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe vision of a flying roll.1–4The vision of a woman and an ephah.5–11
The flying scroll (verses 1–4)

The Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments are scrolls, in which God has written the great truths of his law and gospel.

They are flying scrolls: the Lord sends his word swiftly (Psalm 147:15).

This vision reveals his righteous anger against sin.

If only we could see, by faith, the curse of God's law hanging over the guilty world like a dark storm cloud, shutting out the warmth of divine favor and ready to break in thunder and lightning!

Then how welcome we would find the news of the Savior who redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us!

Sin destroys homes and families, particularly when people hurt others or give false testimony.

Nothing can shut out God's judgment—not locks, bars or walls.

Some of its consequences ruin a person's earthly possessions; others reach the soul and lead to everlasting punishment.

We have all transgressed God's law.

We therefore have no escape from its judgment except to flee for refuge to the hope announced in the gospel.

The woman inside the ephah (verses 5–11)

Zechariah saw an ephah, a container shaped like a measure used for grain.

Henry takes this as a picture of the Jewish nation filling up the measure of its iniquity.

When that measure was full, God would allow its enemies to take it captive as punishment.

The woman seated inside represents, in Henry's interpretation, the Jewish church and nation in a later corrupt period.

The heavy lead cover expresses the guilt weighing upon a sinner, carrying the unrepentant toward judgment.

Henry further understands the vision as foretelling the condemnation and dispersion of the Jews after the crucifixion of Christ and the rejection of his gospel.

The container carried into a distant land would picture their removal from their country and prolonged life elsewhere, as in the earlier captivity to Babylon.

Henry considers this later period of suffering much longer than the Babylonian exile, and interprets the picture in terms of Israel's blindness and unbelief.

These are Henry's historical and theological identifications, not independent findings or a silent revision of Scripture.

The universal application is to beware of storing up wrath for judgment.

Every crime added to the record fills the measure further.
